How to Play King of Tokyo: Rules That Click in One Round

2026-09-30

How to play King of Tokyo: pick a giant monster, roll six dice up to three times, and be the last one standing or the first to 20 victory points. It plays 2 to 6 people in about 30 minutes, ages 8 and up. That is the whole game. The catch is that the best move is often the most boring one, and your brain will fight you on it.

I taught this game to a full table at a birthday party last month, and here is what happened. The loudest player rolled three claws and knocked everyone out of the game by round six, while the quietest player sat outside Tokyo hoarding energy cubes. The quiet player won. Everybody assumed the punchy monster was winning because it was the one making all the noise. That is the trap, and this whole game is built around it.

King of Tokyo looks like a Yahtzee fistfight. It is not. It is king of the hill wearing a monster costume, and the hill is the whole strategy. Once you see that, the rules take about five minutes and the game opens right up.

Setup: Pick Your Monster, This Is the Whole Board

Everyone chooses a monster and takes the matching board. Your board has two tracks on it: life points on top and victory points on the bottom. You start at 10 life and 0 points. Shuffle the power card deck, reveal three cards face up, and place the energy cubes and the black die within reach. Set the green dice aside; they are for the 2-player variant.

Then roll to see who goes first. Whoever rolls the most claws (smash symbols) starts, and on your very first turn you move into the center of the board. That circle in the middle is Tokyo. The first player is forced to enter it, and that one decision sets up everything that follows.

The Turn: Roll, Keep, Reroll, Like Yahtzee

If you have played Yahtzee, you already know the rhythm. You roll six dice. You set aside the ones you like, and you reroll the rest. You can do this twice, so you get up to three rolls total, then you score what you have. Every die has five possible symbols.

The numbers 1, 2, and 3 score victory points, but only in sets. Roll three of a kind and you score the number on the die, so three 3s is 3 points. Every extra matching die adds one more, so four 3s is 4 points. A claw is your attack. A heart is your heal. A bolt is energy, and energy buys power cards.

Here is the key insight for turn one. Most beginners roll the dice and try to cram in as many points as possible. That is usually wrong. At the start of the game, nobody is in danger, so hearts are worthless and energy looks useless. The dice give you what fits the situation, but you get to steer which situation you want. Deciding what you are rolling for matters more than what lands.

What Each Die Face Actually Does

Claws are your attack, and their target depends on where you stand. If you are inside Tokyo, every claw you roll deals 1 damage to every monster outside it, all at once. If you are outside Tokyo, every claw deals 1 damage only to the monster sitting inside Tokyo. Being in Tokyo makes you the target of everyone's claws. Being outside makes your claws reach only the king.

This is the rule that makes the whole game work. The monster in Tokyo is a magnet. Every other player's claws are pointed at it, and it cannot heal at all. Hearts let you recover 1 life each, but only if you are outside Tokyo. Inside the city, hearts do nothing for you. You are stuck out front taking hits, and the only way out is to take damage and choose to yield the space, or get knocked to zero.

Pay attention to this number: 2. Whenever you enter Tokyo, you instantly gain 1 victory point. And if you start your turn still sitting inside Tokyo, you gain 2 more. That is your payoff for being the target. The points on the king's track climb fast, and that is exactly what lures the whole table into attacking it.

The Math of the Monster in the Middle

So here is the balancing act. Being in Tokyo gives you free victory points every round, at the price of being the only target at the table and being unable to heal. Being outside Tokyo lets you heal, but you score nothing unless you are punching the king.

Energy is the third path, and mostly ignored by new players. Every bolt you roll gives you one energy cube, and energy buys power cards. Power cards are the hidden engine of the game. Some are one-use effects, but the keep ones sit in front of you forever, and they are how you win from a position of weakness. A card that gives you 2 victory points at the end of every round beats any single lucky roll you will ever make.

At five or six players, the board opens a second space, Tokyo Bay, next to the main city. Same rule: it counts as being in Tokyo, you score points there, you cannot heal there. The spaces just split the target so nobody takes every hit on the whole table. Under four players it closes again, and there is only one hill.

Here is the part nobody tells you: the player winning the game is the one the table is losing to, not the one up in points. I watched a grown man sit outside Tokyo for six straight turns, take exactly three hits, and quietly buy two keep cards that math'd out to more points than the monster that had been screaming at us all game. The loud monster in Tokyo looks like it is winning because its point track is high and its fists are everywhere. But it cannot heal, every claw on the table is aimed at it, and one bad roll puts it at zero. King of Tokyo is not a fighting game disguised as a dice game. It is a chicken game. The first person to flinch and jump back into the brawl usually hands the win to whoever stayed patient. I lost my first four games this exact way before a friend finally said it out loud: stop treating Tokyo like a prize. It is a chair that everyone wants you to sit in.

The Win, and the Two Player Variant

The game ends one of two ways. Reach 20 victory points and you are the King of Tokyo, full stop. Or be the last monster still standing after everyone else hits zero life and gets knocked out. That is the whole win condition, and it is why energy into power cards works: it is a path to cross the 20 line without ever winning a single fight.

With exactly two players, the rules swap points for energy. Entering Tokyo gives you 1 energy instead of a point, and starting your turn in Tokyo gives you 1 energy instead of 2 points. It plays fine, but it is clearly a workaround. This is a game for a table, not a date night. If you only ever have two people, this is not the game I would hand you first.

What to Buy, and What to Skip

So now you know how to play. The real choice is which box reaches your table on game night.

The King of Tokyo New Edition is the box everyone means. It handles 2 to 6 players, runs about 30 minutes, and throws in a bonus mime monster plus the black die, which lands a special face that smacks every other monster at once. It is the full details on my King of Tokyo page. If your group loves it, the Power Up expansion is the one worth owning, because it gives every monster its own evolution deck and fixes the one real weakness this game has. Skip Dark and the monster packs until the base game feels solved. That took me maybe eight plays.

And if the dice-roll core does not fit your group, King of Tokyo Dark is the same system with a meaner, more tactical coat of paint, and Sushi Go! jumps in faster, under $12, if you only have fifteen minutes.

The Honest Truth About King of Tokyo

The first game is a bit of a blur. Six dice, five symbols, a board that is just two numbers and a circle, and the turn order is surprisingly fast, so new players spend the first few rounds trying to read the dice instead of thinking. Nobody has a slow turn, which is great, but it also means there is no time to recover from a misread before it is your roll again.

But here is the other side. By round three of your first game, you get it. The power cards are the only part that demands a second read, and the keep-versus-discard choice is obvious once you have seen one of each. This is the rare game where the teach is genuinely one round, not one session. That is why it has sat on our shelf for years while boxes twice its size have come and gone.

Here is the Shelf Test. Would this game survive 10 plays on your shelf? Ten, yes. Twenty, easily. It is the game I reach for when the table is four to six people, half of them have never played anything past Uno, and someone needs to win their first modern board game without memorizing a rulebook. The New Edition lists at $59.99 and bounces between about $38 and $48 on Amazon; I have watched it sit at $43 for weeks at a time. Under $45 is a fair deal, and it has been known to dip under $40 on a sale. Grab it, teach the round above, and let the patient monster win.
